text:
HR@10 against 99 uniform negatives measures success among 100 candidates; it does not estimate full-catalog HR@10 directly. Krichene and Rendle show that sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation. Keep the pinned evaluator unchanged and qualify conclusions as improvements under its sampled protocol; they do not establish better full-catalog recommendations. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For uncertainty, a suitable application of paired bootstrap is to resample users within each category, retaining both models’ hit indicators together, then recompute the difference between their four-category macro averages. Report a 95% interval for that difference. Pairing preserves user correspondence, as described in [SciPy’s bootstrap documentation](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html). With candidates and trained models fixed, this estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on those choices; it excludes negative-sampling and training-seed variability. One changed hit among 200 users changes category HR by 0.5 percentage points and the four-category macro average by 0.125 points.

Repeated checkpoint/hyperparameter selection on the same validation users can produce optimistic winning scores; an ordinary post-selection bootstrap interval does not correct that search bias. Record selection frequency and treat validation gains as provisional until the host’s independent held-out evaluation. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) establish this general selection-bias problem. Mathematically, raw positive–negative logit margins are scale-dependent: multiplying scores by a positive constant enlarges margins without changing ranks. Average pairwise margins also miss the top-10 boundary: a positive can beat most negatives yet rank eleventh. Use margins as diagnostics alongside measured hits and ranks, never as substitutes for HR@10.
